leadRef: Lean experts certify the Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
description: The Lean and Mathlib communities certify Levent Alpöge's Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis; Dragos finds AI providers leaking prompts; Microsoft discloses an exploited Entra flaw; Amazon nears a $7.5bn Decart deal; Spain extends its bank levy.

thirtySecond.p: Two million planted secrets show breached AI hosts, resellers keeping prompts and zero-retention settings ignored.
Microsoft says attackers read admin emails and tenant data through Entra Connect Health for months before a 19 Nov fix.
Sánchez will extend the bank tax through 2027 and put about €1.4bn into housing, a week before the election.

footerNote: Sunday's deep beat, the week in storylines: AI doing maths went from claim to certified proof in a day; the AI supply chain (prompts, hosted models, identity services, Kubernetes clouds) was the week's security theme; prediction markets and crypto rules kept moving through courts and legislatures; and the AI sell-off left Nvidia's leadership fight unresolved.

stories.title: Dragos (HD Moore, 19 Nov) says nearly two million prompts seeded with unique URLs and canary credentials, sent to AI services from July to November, show attackers stealing data from at least three AI hosting providers, inference-marketplace resellers viewing and keeping customer prompts, and providers ignoring zero-data-retention settings, with some prompts reaching Chinese organisations; separately Prime Intellect discloses that an unauthorised party swapped its DeepSeek V4.1 Flash deployment for a refusal-stripped copy for 53 hours (8-10 Nov)
stories.h: Planted secrets show AI providers leaking prompts, and one host's model was secretly swapped
stories.ticker: Dragos: 2M canary prompts show 3 AI hosts breached, resellers keeping prompts; Prime Intellect model swapped for 53h
stories.body:
Dragos's research team, led by HD Moore, sent about two million prompts containing unique URLs and fake credentials to widely used AI services between July and November, then watched where they surfaced. It found attackers actively stealing data from three hosting providers (the earliest from mid-July); bait AWS keys were used for tens of thousands of API calls, and one attacker who had hit two providers at once added the ARTEX AI hacking tool on 1 November. Resellers on an inference marketplace could read and keep customer prompts using ordinary logging, and several providers appeared to ignore privacy settings, including zero data retention: prompts sent to US providers reached Chinese organisations, and one seeded link turned up in an internal company chat in China. Dragos does not name the providers in the sections we read. Separately, Prime Intellect discloses that an unauthorised party replaced its DeepSeek V4.1 Flash deployment with a copy modified to stop refusing, from 8 Nov 01:24 to 10 Nov 06:35 UTC; HarmBench refusals fell from 198 of 240 to zero while capability scores were unchanged. It says it found no sign prompts were recorded. The Defiant reports Together AI disclosed a prompt leak after the study; we could not open that report.

So what: banks sending customer or deal data to AI models through routers, marketplaces or small hosts should assume a privacy flag is not a control. Map every route a prompt takes, prefer direct contracts with named providers, and seed your own canaries.
stories.chip: Opened Dragos's report and Prime Intellect's security advisory (both official), plus CryptoSlate's write-up of the swap and Ars Technica's security page; The Defiant (Together AI) was blocked.
src: Dragos: Three breaches, endless leaks: your AI supply chain needs canaries
Prime Intellect: notice regarding deepseek-v4.1-flash, 8 to 10 November
CryptoSlate: hackers swapped a hosted DeepSeek model for 53 hours
Ars Technica security (Dan Goodin, 20 Nov: researcher plants 2m canaries)
The Defiant: Together AI discloses prompt leak after Dragos study (not opened)
Hacker News: OpenRouter prompts to MiniMax may have been read
stories.short: Dragos seeded about two million prompts with fake credentials and found attackers stealing data from three AI hosting providers, resellers keeping customer prompts and zero-retention settings ignored. Separately, Prime Intellect says a hacker swapped its DeepSeek model for a refusal-free copy for 53 hours. The affected providers in Dragos's study are not named.

stat.label: canary prompts Dragos sent to AI services

stories.title: Microsoft notifies organisations (20 Nov) that attackers exploited a flaw in the Entra Connect Health API, introduced 23 Jul and found 9 Nov, to read tenant metadata including administrator and technical-contact email addresses, tenant IDs, domains, licence tiers and sync status, plus an expired certificate; fixed 19 Nov; no passwords, tokens or valid keys exposed, Microsoft says (BleepingComputer, 21 Nov)
stories.h: Microsoft says attackers read tenant data through a flaw in Entra Connect Health
stories.ticker: Microsoft: Entra Connect Health API flaw exploited; admin emails and tenant metadata read; fixed 19 Nov
stories.body:
Microsoft is telling customers that attackers exploited a vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API, the cloud service that monitors on-premises identity servers, according to a notification shared by admins and reported by BleepingComputer. The flaw was introduced on 23 July, found on 9 November and fixed server-side on 19 November. Microsoft says attackers got read-only access to tenant metadata: email addresses of administrators and technical contacts, tenant IDs and names, domains, country and region, Entra licence tier and directory-sync status, plus an expired certificate once used to register Connect Health agents. It says no passwords, hashes, tokens, valid keys, Active Directory topology or Azure subscription data were exposed and no configuration changes were found. It has not said how many tenants were hit; several managed service providers received notices for multiple customers. No customer action is required, the notice says.

So what: banks running hybrid identity should check the Microsoft 365 admin centre for the notice and expect targeted phishing at the named admin addresses; the data is a map of who runs your identity stack.
stories.chip: Opened BleepingComputer's report, which quotes Microsoft's customer notification; no public Microsoft advisory found on re-search.
src: BleepingComputer: Microsoft Entra Connect Health flaw exploited to steal tenant data
stories.short: Microsoft says attackers exploited a flaw in its Entra Connect Health service, live from 23 July until a fix on 19 November, to read tenant metadata such as admin email addresses, tenant IDs and licence details. It says no passwords, tokens or valid keys were exposed. Only one outlet has reported the customer notice so far.

stat.label: the flaw was live, 23 Jul to 19 Nov

stories.title: Amazon is nearing a deal to buy Decart, the three-year-old Israeli startup behind the Lucy real-time video model and Oasis world models used to simulate worlds for robots and self-driving systems, for about $7.5bn, the FT reports (21 Nov); the WSJ first reported talks at about $7bn; Decart was valued near $4bn in May
stories.h: Amazon nears a $7.5bn deal for Decart, maker of real-time video and world models
stories.ticker: Amazon nears ~$7.5bn purchase of Decart (Lucy video, Oasis world models), FT reports
stories.body:
Amazon is nearing a deal to buy Decart, an Israeli AI startup, for about $7.5bn, the Financial Times reported on Saturday (via The Information). The Wall Street Journal first reported talks last month at around $7bn. The product is the point: Decart's Lucy model edits video in real time, and its Oasis models generate simulated worlds used to train and test robots and self-driving systems. PitchBook data cited by the WSJ put Decart near $4bn in May, after a $300m round led by Radical Ventures that brought in Nvidia. Earlier reports said other buyers had looked and walked away. Neither company has confirmed a deal.

So what: world models are becoming a cloud product; if AWS buys one, expect simulation and synthetic-video tools inside its AI stack, and more pressure on rivals' prices for the few teams that build them.
stories.chip: Opened The Information's briefing (headline and FT attribution) and Finimize's summary of the WSJ report; the FT article itself is paywalled.
src: The Information: Amazon nearing $7.5 billion purchase of Decart (citing the FT)
Finimize: Amazon reportedly in talks to buy Decart (citing the WSJ)
stories.short: Amazon is close to buying Decart, the Israeli startup behind the Lucy real-time video model and Oasis world models, for about $7.5bn, the FT reports. Decart was valued near $4bn in May. Neither company has confirmed the deal, which would put world-model technology inside Amazon's cloud.

stories.title: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez says (21 Nov) his cabinet will approve on Tuesday an extension of the banking levy through 2027, raising about €1.4bn that will go entirely to housing (social housing, tenant incentives and renovation), eight days before the 29 Nov snap election (Reuters)
stories.h: Spain will extend its bank levy through 2027 to pay for housing, Sánchez says
stories.ticker: Sánchez: Spain's bank levy extended through 2027, ~€1.4bn to housing; cabinet vote Tuesday
stories.body:
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said on Saturday that his cabinet will approve on Tuesday an extension of the current banking levy to 2027 and that its revenue, about €1.4bn, will all go to housing: social housing, incentives for tenants and home renovation, Reuters reports. "We will extend the bank tax, and the revenue will go towards" housing, he said. Sánchez called a snap election for 29 November to ride the momentum of mass housing protests. A government formed after the vote could change course, and the detailed terms have not been published.

So what: Spain's big lenders face another year of the levy in their 2027 plans, and politicians elsewhere are watching a tax on bank income sold as housing money; banks with European franchises should model it.
stories.chip: Opened Reuters' report on Yahoo News and Global Banking & Finance Review's copy; the €1.4bn figure appears in both.
src: Reuters (via Yahoo News): Spain to extend banking tax to fund housing policies, PM says
Global Banking & Finance Review: Spain extends banking tax to fund housing policies until 2027
stories.short: Spain's prime minister Pedro Sánchez says his cabinet will approve on Tuesday an extension of the bank levy through 2027, raising about €1.4bn for social housing, tenant incentives and renovation. The announcement comes eight days before the 29 November snap election, and a new government could change it.

stories.title: Week-long talks at the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva fail (21 Nov) to agree a mandate to negotiate a legally binding treaty on autonomous weapons after all-night sessions, with Russia blocking and the US and other military AI powers reluctant; the conference adopts a weaker mandate to 'elaborate by consensus' an instrument that may carry no legal obligations, although more than 100 states wanted a new law
stories.h: UN talks on a binding treaty for autonomous weapons collapse in Geneva
stories.ticker: UN CCW fails to agree a treaty mandate on autonomous weapons; weaker consensus process adopted
stories.body:
After a week of talks and an all-night session, the UN's Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in Geneva failed just before 5am on Saturday to agree a mandate to negotiate a legally binding treaty on autonomous weapons, the Guardian reports. More than 100 states wanted a new law, but the forum works by consensus. Russia led the objections with stalling tactics, and the US and other powers investing in AI warfare, including South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany, preferred a nonbinding approach. The conference instead asked countries "to elaborate by consensus" an instrument that may carry no legal obligations. The US said human control over such weapons came up between Xi Jinping and Donald Trump at Apec this week.

So what: there will be no global legal limit on AI that selects and attacks targets for years; defence-tech lending and investment will keep running on national rules and company policies.
stories.chip: Opened the Guardian's report from Geneva and The Verge's write-up.
src: The Guardian: international UN talks on controlling autonomous weapons collapse
The Verge: the UN fails to agree on rules regulating 'killer robots'
stories.short: UN talks in Geneva failed to agree a mandate for a binding treaty on autonomous weapons after an all-night session. More than 100 states wanted one, but Russia blocked consensus and the US and other military powers preferred nonbinding rules. Countries will instead work on an instrument that may carry no legal obligations.

stat.label: states that wanted a binding treaty

stories.title: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, the database police use for warrants, missing persons and stolen property, CNN reports (21 Nov), the second reported FBI breach in two months; Trump confirms the hack to Fox News; NBC and Reuters report a separate intrusion into a US Department of Agriculture payments database that is disrupting farm payments
stories.h: FBI's national crime database and a USDA payments system are reported hacked
stories.ticker: FBI probes apparent breach of NCIC crime database; USDA payments system also hacked
stories.body:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center (NCIC), the database police across the US use during traffic stops and investigations to check warrants, missing persons, stolen vehicles and protection orders, CNN reported, citing two people briefed. It is the second reported FBI breach in two months, after ShinyHunters claimed an attack through an Oracle PeopleSoft flaw. It is not known when or how attackers got in, or whether data was taken; President Trump confirmed the hack in a Fox News interview. Separately, NBC and Reuters report an intrusion into a US Department of Agriculture payments database, which former officials warn could open a path to more sensitive data; local reports say farm payments are disrupted as a 11 December sign-up deadline nears.

So what: banks that rely on government data feeds or pay out farm and subsidy money should watch for delays and fraud attempts that exploit the confusion.
stories.chip: Opened BleepingComputer's report (citing CNN) and The Verge's weekend round-up (citing NBC, Reuters and Fox News).
src: BleepingComputer: FBI reportedly hacked again, this time targeting nationwide police database
The Verge: the FBI and USDA were reportedly hacked
stories.short: The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its National Crime Information Center, the database police use to check warrants and stolen property, CNN reports; it is the second reported FBI breach in two months. A separate hack of a US agriculture payments database is disrupting farm payments. How attackers got in is unknown.

stat.label: reported FBI breach in two months

stories.title: Rackspace tells customers (notice reported 21 Nov) that an unauthorised party used leaked credentials to access its Rackspace Spot Kubernetes cloud from about 00:20 to 22:00 UTC on 17 Nov, acting as users in some customer organisations to create pods, read Kubernetes Secrets and list nodes and volumes; customers must rotate Spot API and refresh tokens and every credential stored in cluster Secrets
stories.h: Rackspace Spot breach let attackers read customers' Kubernetes secrets for most of a day
stories.ticker: Rackspace Spot breached with leaked credentials on 17 Nov; customers told to rotate all cluster secrets
stories.body:
Rackspace says an unauthorised party used leaked credentials to get into parts of Rackspace Spot, its managed Kubernetes cloud, from about 00:20 to 22:00 UTC on 17 November, according to a customer notice obtained by BleepingComputer. Acting as legitimate users in some customer organisations, the attackers could create pods, read Kubernetes Secrets (where apps keep database passwords, API keys and tokens) and list nodes and volumes, and could have read any Spot API or refresh token the user held. Rackspace learned of it from a customer on 18 November, revoked tokens, removed the pods and rotated keys. It tells customers to reissue tokens, download fresh configs, rotate every credential stored in cluster Secrets and review logs for databases, registries, Git and cloud storage back to 17 November.

So what: a breach at a cloud host becomes a breach of every system whose keys sat in its clusters; vendor-risk teams should ask Kubernetes providers how quickly they can force secret rotation.
stories.chip: Opened BleepingComputer's report quoting the customer notice and indicators of compromise; no Rackspace public post found.
src: BleepingComputer: Rackspace Spot breach let hackers access customer Kubernetes secrets
stories.short: Rackspace says attackers used leaked credentials to get into its Rackspace Spot Kubernetes cloud for most of 17 November, where they could create pods and read customers' Kubernetes Secrets, which hold passwords and API keys. Customers are told to rotate every stored credential. Only one outlet has the notice so far.

stories.title: Security firm NebuSec shows (published 20 Nov) that a malicious webpage opened by Meta's Muse personal agent could pull a user's conversation history and stored memories to an outside server without any approval prompt, and that chaining a flaw in Muse's built-in browser to a Linux kernel bug gave full control of the user's cloud machine, including its credential store and the Sentinel monitoring layer; a lab demonstration, now fixed, NebuSec says (The Hacker News, 21 Nov)
stories.h: Researchers show one malicious webpage could hijack Meta's Muse agent and its stored logins
stories.ticker: NebuSec: one webpage could make Meta's Muse leak chats and reach stored credentials; fixed
stories.body:
Researchers at NebuSec showed that a malicious webpage opened by Meta's Muse, the personal agent that works through users' connected accounts and can make purchases, could copy a user's conversation history and stored memories to an outside server and alter them with no approval prompt, The Hacker News reports. They then chained a flaw in Muse's built-in browser to a Linux kernel bug to take full control of the user's cloud machine, reaching the credential store, saved files and Sentinel, the monitoring layer meant to be the single gate for what the agent sends out. It was a lab demonstration inside the researchers' own accounts, not an attack on users, and NebuSec says Meta has fixed every weakness it describes. Earlier this week Meta staff found Muse surfacing strangers' bank balances in internal tests.

So what: agents that hold customers' bank logins are now a target in their own right; banks should treat agent platforms as third parties with access to accounts and press for proof of isolation.
stories.chip: Opened The Hacker News report, which links NebuSec's write-up and technical breakdown; we did not open NebuSec's own pages.
src: The Hacker News: a single malicious webpage let researchers hijack Meta Muse
stories.short: Security firm NebuSec showed that one malicious webpage could make Meta's Muse agent send a user's chats and memories to an outside server without asking, and that chained bugs gave full control of the user's cloud machine and its stored logins. It was a lab test, and NebuSec says Meta has fixed every flaw.

stat.label: all flaws, NebuSec says; lab-only test

stories.title: GnuPG releases GPGME 2.3.1 (20 Nov) to fix CVE-2026-129975, a critical double free in all earlier versions that an OpenPGP key with a very long user ID can trigger, letting attackers exfiltrate data from mail clients, XMPP clients, Samba, Gpg4win and other apps that use the library, with remote code execution not ruled out; disclosure was moved up from 25 Nov because of Ruby2Shell; separately pwn.ai publishes Upload2Shell (CVE-2026-125396), a Ghostscript sandbox escape fixed in 10.08.0
stories.h: GnuPG patches a critical GPGME bug that a booby-trapped key can trigger
stories.ticker: CVE-2026-129975: critical GPGME double free; update to 2.3.1 and new Gpg4win
stories.body:
The GnuPG project released GPGME 2.3.1 on Friday to fix CVE-2026-129975, which it calls a critical bug in all earlier versions. An OpenPGP key with a crafted, very long user ID triggers a double free in two routines that read output from gpg; the project says this can be used to exfiltrate data from applications, for example by sending signed data, and that remote code execution can't be ruled out. GPGME is the library most mail clients, many XMPP clients, Samba and GnuPG's own Gpg4win and GnuPG Desktop use to talk to GnuPG; new versions of those were released too. Johan Carlsson found it and GitLab reported it on 12 November; disclosure moved up from 25 November because GitLab had to ship early for the Ruby2Shell bug. No attacks are reported. Separately, pwn.ai published Upload2Shell (CVE-2026-125396), a Ghostscript sandbox escape reachable through document and image uploads, fixed upstream in Ghostscript 10.08.0 in September.

So what: banks use GnuPG for file transfers with counterparties and regulators; patch GPGME and Gpg4win on transfer servers and desktops now.
stories.chip: Opened the GnuPG security advisory (official), The Hacker News report and pwn.ai's Upload2Shell page.
src: GnuPG: security advisory for GPGME (T8557, CVE-2026-129975)
The Hacker News: GnuPG warns critical GPGME flaw could expose app data
Hacker News: RCE in GnuPG (228 points)
stories.short: GnuPG released GPGME 2.3.1 to fix CVE-2026-129975, a critical bug in every earlier version: a booby-trapped OpenPGP key can make apps that use the library leak data, and code execution can't be ruled out. Mail clients, Samba and Gpg4win are affected. No attacks are reported yet.

stories.title: A federal judge in Manhattan denies (20 Nov) the CFTC's second emergency bid to stop New York Attorney General Letitia James's case against Kalshi, sending to a New York state court on Monday (23 Nov) a proposed order that Kalshi says would shut its exchange nationwide; James, who sued in July alleging unlicensed gambling, says shutting it is not her goal
stories.h: Kalshi faces a Monday hearing on a New York order it says would shut it down
stories.ticker: Judge rejects CFTC bid; NY state court hears order Kalshi says would shut its exchange on Monday
stories.body:
A federal judge in Manhattan on Friday denied the CFTC's second emergency request to stop New York Attorney General Letitia James from pursuing her case against Kalshi, sending the fight to a New York state court on Monday, Crypto Briefing reports. That court will weigh an order that Kalshi says would shut down its exchange nationwide, since the company is headquartered in New York; James has said that is not her goal, per The Block. Her July lawsuit alleges Kalshi runs unlicensed gambling under state law. It adds to appeals-court losses for Kalshi in other states this month.

So what: brokers and banks partnering with prediction markets face a real chance that the biggest US venue is restricted by a state court before federal rules settle.
stories.chip: Opened Crypto Briefing's report; The Block and CoinDesk headlines carry the same Monday hearing (both blocked).
src: Crypto Briefing: Kalshi faces New York court hearing on order that could shut down its exchange
The Block: Kalshi faces Monday hearing on New York order
stories.short: A federal judge rejected the CFTC's second emergency bid to halt New York's case against Kalshi, so a state court will hear on Monday an order Kalshi says would shut its exchange nationwide. New York's attorney general says that is not her aim. The case alleges unlicensed gambling.

stories.title: Mexican forces, working with US intelligence, capture cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, 'El Chapo Isidro', one of the FBI's ten most wanted, in Guasave, Sinaloa, after an overnight firefight (21 Nov); at least 11 people, including seven alleged gunmen and four others, die in the violence that follows (AP)
stories.h: Mexico captures FBI-wanted cartel boss 'El Chapo Isidro'; at least 11 killed
stories.ticker: Mexico captures 'El Chapo Isidro' Meza Flores with US intelligence help; at least 11 dead in Sinaloa
stories.body:
Mexican forces captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro" and one of the FBI's ten most wanted fugitives, in Guasave, Sinaloa, and flew him to Mexico City on Saturday after a heavy overnight firefight that left trucks and businesses burning, AP reports. The operation was run by Mexico's defence ministry with US intelligence agencies. At least 11 people died in the violence, including seven alleged cartel gunmen. Meza Flores rose through the Beltrán-Leyva cartel before leading his own group.

So what: a high-profile US-Mexico security win as the US presses Mexico on cartels; expect retaliation risk in Sinaloa and possible extradition moves.
stories.chip: Opened AP's report in The Hindu and the Guardian's report; NYT, DW, France 24 and Al Jazeera also carry it.
src: AP (via The Hindu): 11 killed in burst of violence in northern Mexico after capture of Meza Flores
The Guardian: alleged Mexican drug cartel boss El Chapo Isidro arrested
The New York Times: how Mexico captured a most wanted man
stories.short: Mexican forces, helped by US intelligence, captured cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, 'El Chapo Isidro', one of the FBI's ten most wanted, in Sinaloa after an overnight gun battle. At least 11 people died in the violence that followed. He was flown to Mexico City.

stat.label: killed in Sinaloa after the capture

stories.title: COP31 in Antalya runs more than a day over time and is suspended for the night (21 Nov) in deadlock: the EU and Pacific islands reject a draft with no reference to cutting fossil-fuel demand, the Africa Group wants more adaptation money the EU will not back, delegates move flights to Monday, and the summit could end without a deal for only the second time since 1995 (BBC)
stories.h: COP31 climate talks deadlock over fossil fuels and run past their deadline
stories.ticker: COP31 deadlocked a day past deadline; EU says 'no deal' without fossil-fuel language
stories.body:
Talks at COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, were in deadlock and suspended for the night on Saturday after running more than a day over time, the BBC reports. The EU and Pacific island nations are pushing back against a draft that makes no reference to reducing demand for fossil fuels; EU climate commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said that without "what is needed" there is "no deal". The Africa Group wants more money for adaptation, which the EU has said it will not support. Negotiators due to fly home on Sunday moved flights to Monday. Without consensus the summit could end with no deal and reconvene next year, which has happened only once since 1995. An earlier draft, Reuters reported, had dropped language on phasing out fossil fuels.

So what: a weak or failed COP removes a push behind transition-finance targets; banks with net-zero lending commitments face less policy cover and more scrutiny.
stories.chip: Opened the BBC's report from Antalya; Arab News carried Reuters' account of the revised draft.
src: BBC: fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock
Arab News (Reuters): COP31 draft climate deal removes mention of fossil fuels
stories.short: COP31 in Turkey ran more than a day past its deadline and was suspended in deadlock. The EU and Pacific islands reject a draft with no mention of cutting fossil-fuel demand, and African countries want more adaptation money. Without consensus the summit could end with no deal, only the second time since 1995.

stories.title: Hong Kong publishes (20 Nov) the Virtual Asset Services Legislation (Amendment) Bill 2026, requiring firms that deal, advise, manage or provide custody for crypto assets to be licensed by or registered with the SFC, with first reading in the Legislative Council on 2 Dec
stories.h: Hong Kong bill would license crypto custodians, dealers and advisers
stories.ticker: Hong Kong bill brings crypto dealing, advice, management and custody under SFC licensing; first reading 2 Dec
stories.body:
Hong Kong's government published the Virtual Asset Services Legislation (Amendment) Bill 2026 on Friday, which would require firms doing four activities, dealing, advising, managing and custody of crypto assets, to be licensed by or registered with the SFC, extending oversight beyond trading platforms, Cointelegraph reports. Providers would face fit-and-proper checks under the anti-money-laundering ordinance. First reading in the Legislative Council is set for 2 December.

So what: banks offering crypto custody or advice in Hong Kong will need to map their activities onto the new licence categories.
stories.chip: Opened Cointelegraph's report; CryptoRank and The Coin Republic carry the same four categories.
src: Cointelegraph: Hong Kong proposes licensing for crypto custodians and advisers

stories.title: PayPal CEO Enrique Lores installs a new management team (20 Nov) and says CFO and COO Jamie Miller, once interim CEO, will leave on 1 Feb, as he tries to restart profitable growth after three CEOs in three years (Banking Dive, Payments Dive)
stories.h: PayPal's CEO replaces his top team as CFO Jamie Miller prepares to leave
stories.ticker: PayPal names new managers; CFO/COO Jamie Miller to leave 1 Feb
stories.body:
PayPal CEO Enrique Lores, in the job since March, named a new set of top managers on Friday and said Jamie Miller, chief financial and operating officer and once interim CEO, will leave; she stays until 1 February, according to a filing, Banking Dive reports. The reshuffle is meant to restart profitable growth at a company that has had three CEOs in as many years.

So what: a new finance chief will set PayPal's 2027 plan as agentic checkout from OpenAI, Google and the card networks competes for the same transactions.
stories.chip: Opened Banking Dive's report, which cites PayPal's press release and filing.
src: Banking Dive: PayPal CEO remakes team

stories.title: Samsung names Sang Joon Hwang, who led DRAM and HBM development, president and head of its memory business and Won-Joon Choi head of the Galaxy mobile unit (20 Nov), with co-CEOs Young Hyun Jun and TM Roh staying on, in a week when it reportedly paused some chip shipments to China under new US export rules (FT via TNW)
stories.h: Samsung puts its HBM chief in charge of memory amid a reported China shipment pause
stories.ticker: Samsung: Sang Joon Hwang to run memory, Won-Joon Choi mobile; China chip shipments reportedly paused
stories.body:
Samsung Electronics promoted Sang Joon Hwang, who led memory development including the HBM used in AI chips, to president and head of the memory business, and named Won-Joon Choi head of Mobile eXperience, the Galaxy phone unit, its newsroom says. Co-CEOs Young Hyun Jun and TM Roh keep their roles. Sangyeun Cho becomes head of System LSI. The changes came in a week when Samsung reportedly paused some chip shipments to China under new US export rules, TNW notes, citing the Financial Times.

So what: Samsung is betting its memory turnaround on an HBM engineer as AI memory prices drive its profits.
stories.chip: Opened Samsung's newsroom announcement and TNW's report.
src: Samsung Newsroom: Samsung Electronics announces new leadership
TNW: Samsung names new chip and phone bosses amid a reported China shipment halt

stories.title: SK Hynix will become Kioxia's largest shareholder with an indirect stake of about 14.1% by converting ¥129bn ($810m) of bonds held since the 2018 Toshiba memory deal into shares and buying Bain's remaining SPC2 shares, its filing says (20 Nov); steps close in December (Bloomberg, TNW)
stories.h: SK Hynix will become Kioxia's largest shareholder by converting old bonds
stories.ticker: SK Hynix to hold ~14.1% of Kioxia after converting ¥129bn of bonds
stories.body:
SK Hynix will become the largest shareholder of Kioxia, its Japanese flash-memory rival, with an indirect stake of about 14.1%, by converting ¥129bn ($810m) of bonds it has held since 2018 into shares of SPC2, the vehicle from the Toshiba memory deal, and buying Bain Capital's remaining SPC2 shares, its filing says. That puts it ahead of Toshiba (10.46%). The steps close in December.

So what: the HBM leader gains more say over a major NAND maker as AI servers drive demand for both kinds of memory.
stories.chip: Opened TNW's report, which cites the filing and Bloomberg.
src: TNW: SK Hynix will become Kioxia's largest shareholder through a bond swap

stories.title: Tesla starts rolling out FSD v15 (21 Nov) with an upgraded vision encoder shared with Robotaxi and Optimus that it says cuts critical interventions 25x, a new 'Tesla Augmented Reality' end-to-end visualisation, and fixes for sign detection, potholes and school-zone speeds; it has not said which cars get it first (Electrek)
stories.h: Tesla begins rolling out FSD v15 and claims a 25x drop in critical interventions
stories.ticker: Tesla FSD v15 rolling out: shared vision encoder, AR visualisation, 25x intervention claim
stories.body:
Tesla has started rolling out FSD v15, Electrek reports, citing Tesla's release notes. It adds an upgraded vision encoder shared with Robotaxi and Optimus, trained on millions of internet videos, which Tesla says improves the critical intervention rate 25 times, plus a new Tesla Augmented Reality visualisation and fixes aimed at sign detection, potholes and school-zone speeds. Tesla has not said which vehicles get it first. The 25x figure is Tesla's own.

So what: Tesla's claims arrive just as Waymo pauses freeway rides; regulators will want data, not release notes.

A team from ByteDance and several US universities argues that agent training pipelines have become needlessly nested and introduces Axion 1.0, an agent model trained in just three phases that it says rivals top commercial models on benchmarks, crediting carefully curated data rather than more training steps, The Decoder reports. stories.body:
Ubisoft has launched Motherbrain, a subsidiary developing proprietary generative AI for gameplay, announced with its first-half results, GamesIndustry.biz reports. It is focused on "smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds", is staffed by the team behind its Teammates project, and aims to serve creators beyond Ubisoft. The launch comes as Ubisoft lays off 166 staff at its Montreal and Quebec studios.

So what: big publishers are turning AI teams into products they can license, while cutting traditional roles.

stories.update: The Lean and Mathlib communities, backed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, certify (21 Nov) that Levent Alpöge's 17-million-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, after independent proof checkers and two statement-matching tools all passed.
stories.title: The Lean and Mathlib communities certify (21 Nov) that Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge's Claude-assisted Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, released 20 Nov as a 17-million-line library depending only on Mathlib, is correct: dozens of people reproduced the build, two tools confirmed it proves Mathlib's own statement of RH, and several independent kernels (including con-leche and con-ron, which carry formal proofs that they cannot accept a false proof) accepted the exported proof; MIT's Andrew Sutherland publishes a verification log
stories.h: Lean experts certify Anthropic mathematician's Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as correct
stories.sub: A day after Levent Alpöge released a 17-million-line Lean proof, the Lean and Mathlib communities say every check passed. Mathematicians now have to understand the ideas.
stories.ticker: Lean and Mathlib communities certify Alpöge's 17M-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as correct
stories.body:
Yesterday's claim has passed the formal test. In a joint statement endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, the Lean and Mathlib communities say they have full confidence that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct and "hereby certify" both the statement and the proof. The proof is a Lean library of about 17 million lines that depends only on Mathlib. Their checks: the statement of RH is the one already in Mathlib, vetted by Lean and number-theory experts; dozens of people compiled the library and got the same proof export; two independent tools confirmed the theorem proved is exactly Mathlib's RH; and the export was accepted by Lean's own kernel and several independent checkers in different languages, including con-leche and con-ron, which come with formal proofs that they cannot accept a false proof. The checks ran on an inert export, out of reach of any malicious code in the sources. MIT's Andrew Sutherland, who ran his checks with Claude Code, reports all 175,187 modules compile, the five headline theorems use only Lean's three standard axioms, and the nanoda and con-leche kernels accept the full export. The community statement covers RH; it does not mention the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis that Alpöge also claimed, and the human explanation of the new ideas is still to come.

So what: a 167-year-old problem has a machine-checked proof found with an AI model, which is a strong signal that AI plus formal verification can produce results nobody has to take on trust. It does not break today's encryption; the practical lesson for banks is about verification, not cryptography.
stories.chip: Opened the Lean community's joint statement and Andrew Sutherland's MIT verification page; both describe the same checks. Not checked by us: the proof itself.
src: Lean community blog: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
Andrew Sutherland (MIT): verification files for the Lean proof
BBC: an Anthropic worker says he may have cracked the biggest maths problem
Hacker News: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis (802 points)
stories.brief:
On Friday Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said that working with an internal Claude model for about six weeks he had proved the Riemann Hypothesis, and released the proof as Lean code. Normally a claimed proof of a famous conjecture takes referees months or years. Here the proof was written in a language a computer can check, so the question became narrower: does it compile, does it prove the right statement, and can the checker be trusted?

Within a day the Lean and Mathlib communities answered all three. The statement matches the one already in Mathlib; independent people rebuilt the 17-million-line library and got the same export; two tools confirmed the statement; and several independently written checkers, two of them formally proven unable to accept a false proof, accepted it. What remains is human work: understanding why the proof works and what new mathematics it contains.
facts: Formal certification of a Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
Lean and Mathlib communities; Lean FRO; Mathlib Initiative; proof by Levent Alpöge with Claude
Lean kernel, nanoda, con-leche, con-ron, lean4lean; statement compared by two tools
The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis claim; human exposition
stories.impactWho: Mathematicians and AI labs first; for banks and regulators, a signal that formally verified, AI-produced work is becoming practical for high-stakes checks such as code and model verification.
stories.short: The Lean and Mathlib communities certify that Levent Alpöge's 17-million-line Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, made with Anthropic's Claude, is correct. Independent checkers, two formally proven unable to accept a false proof, accepted it. The certificate covers the Riemann Hypothesis, not his separate GRH claim; experts still have to explain the ideas.

stories.h: Trump says Huang should apologise and return to Nvidia; the board says no
stories.ticker: Trump: Huang should apologise and return; board has no plans to bring him back
stories.body:
President Donald Trump said on Friday that Jensen Huang should apologise and be allowed to return as Nvidia's chief executive, DigiTimes reports. Nvidia's board has said plainly it has no plans to bring him back, even as some tech executives push for it, Crypto Briefing notes. Bloomberg reports that California's investigation into whether Nvidia misled investors about China risks now extends to potential criminal violations; we saw only the headline. Nvidia closed the week near $126 after Friday's 14% fall on reports that the SEC is examining its accounting.

So what: political pressure now pulls against the board's governance clean-up; lenders and index investors should expect more volatility until the 10-Q and the board's answers to Treasury arrive.
stories.chip: Opened DigiTimes (lead paragraph; rest paywalled) and Crypto Briefing; the Bloomberg criminal-probe report was seen only as a headline (Seeking Alpha blocked).
